profile.name: Yak dance
profile.tagline: A Himalayan pantomime honoring the yak during the Tibetan New Year.
profile.insight: In 2017, a troupe performing the Yak dance at India’s 68th Republic Day parade in New Delhi won first prize among 22 competing tableaux for their depiction of the mythical discovery of the yak.
profile.profile: The Yak dance, or Yak Chham, is a traditional folk pantomime performed by Mahayana Buddhist tribes in the Himalayan regions of India, including Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, and Ladakh. It features a dancer costumed as a yak carrying a rider, representing the family members who discovered the animal with a magical bird's assistance. The dance serves as a tribute to the yak and is a central feature of the Losar festival, the Tibetan New Year. Its performance is a significant cultural expression, notably showcased on national stages like the Republic Day parade.
profile.profile_long: The Yak dance, known locally as Yak Chham or the Tibetan Yak Dance, is a prominent folk pantomime practiced by Mahayana Buddhist tribes across the Himalayan fringes of India. Its geographical footprint spans the states of Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim, as well as the union territory of Ladakh. The performance is deeply rooted in the cultural identity of these communities, serving as a ritualistic tribute to the yak, an animal essential to the survival and economy of high-altitude Himalayan life. The dance is most notably performed during the Losar festival, which marks the Tibetan New Year, serving as a communal celebration of the animal's historical and spiritual importance. The narrative core of the dance centers on the legend of the Theopa Gali, a family believed to have discovered the yak with the assistance of a magical bird hundreds of years ago. This discovery is re-enacted through the movement of a dancer costumed as the yak, who carries a rider on their back. The performance is not merely a display of movement but a storytelling medium that preserves the oral history of the Mahayana Buddhist tribes. In recent years, the dance has gained national prominence; in 2017, a tableau representing the Yak dance from Arunachal Pradesh was featured at the 68th Republic Day of India celebration at Rajpath, New Delhi. This performance was highly regarded, winning the first prize for the best tableau among 22 participants. Despite its visibility, many technical aspects of the dance, such as the specific musical accompaniment, rhythmic structures, and precise footwork, remain undocumented in current public records. The tradition continues to be a living practice, maintained by the communities of the Himalayan region as a vital link to their ancestral heritage and the mythical origins of their relationship with the yak.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originates from the Mahayana Buddhist tribes of the Himalayas. It commemorates the discovery of the yak by the Theopa Gali family, who were guided by a magical bird hundreds of years ago.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is a pantomime. A dancer wears a yak costume and carries a man on their back, representing the family members who discovered the animal.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dancer wears a yak costume and a mask. It is performed during the Losar festival and was featured at the 68th Republic Day of India in New Delhi.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed to honor the yak and is a key feature of the Losar festival, the Tibetan New Year.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is performed in Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, and Ladakh.
sections.lineage: It is a pantomime of the Mahayana sect of Buddhist Tribes.

profile.sacred_note: Not described in sources as sacred, though it is a pantomime of the Mahayana sect of Buddhist Tribes.
